She kept living with her father in Belo Horizonte, and her mother moved to Recife.
A year later, her father said he had a girlfriend, Juliana, a friendly and generous nurse.
When they got married, Juliana came to live in the apartment with her son, Thiago, who was eight.
For Letícia, living with her stepmother and her father's stepson was very hard.
She thought Thiago was spoiled and noisy, and Juliana a stranger who was bossing her house around.
To her friends, she said that she hated her father's new family.
So she hardly spoke to them and spent the afternoons alone in her room.
Juliana tried to talk, but Letícia was stubborn and always answered with just one word.
One winter night, her father was away on a work trip, and Letícia woke up with a high fever and a sore throat.
She didn't want to ask for help, but she felt so bad that she couldn't even get up.
Thiago heard her coughing and ran to call his mother.
Juliana took her temperature, gave her medicine and spent the whole night beside the bed.
In the morning, she took Letícia to the doctor, who said it was a throat infection.
During the week Letícia was sick, Juliana made soup every day.
Thiago, in turn, left chocolates under her bedroom door.
Little by little, Letícia realized she had been very unpleasant to the two of them.
When her father came back, he found the three of them laughing on the sofa, watching a soap opera.
Today Letícia still calls Juliana by her name, but tells her friends that she gained a second mother.
And Thiago, who before was just her father's stepson, she now calls her brother.

sentences.en: Mariana and Sofia are twin sisters, but they have very different personalities.
Mariana is calm and quiet, while Sofia is restless and a bit stubborn.
Last year, their grandfather died and left an old house in a small town in Minas Gerais as an inheritance.
The house had been built by their great-grandfather, an immigrant who arrived in Brazil almost a hundred years ago.
Felipe, Mariana's husband, is an ambitious businessman.
He thought the sisters should tear down the house and build an apartment building in its place.
"Five years from now, you'll make a lot of money from the apartments," he would say.
Sofia got very angry and said she would never agree to that.
For weeks, the two sisters hardly spoke to each other.
In July, their grandmother, who is a widow and is eighty-two, asked her granddaughters to go with her to the house.

sentences.en: She wanted to tidy up her husband's room before her granddaughters decided anything.
In their grandfather's bedroom, the twins found a suitcase full of old photos and notebooks.
The photos showed parties, birthdays and Sunday lunches in the garden of the house.
In one of the notebooks, their great-grandfather told how he had planted the trees in the garden with his children.
Their grandmother cried and told stories about ancestors they had never known.
That night, Mariana called her husband and explained that she didn't want to lose that history.
Felipe was silent for a few seconds.
Then he admitted that maybe the family needed the house more than the money.
He said they could renovate the house and spend family vacations and holidays there.
Sofia, in turn, apologized to her sister for everything she had said.
This year, the renovation was finished, and the whole family spent the end-of-year holidays at their great-grandfather's house.

sentences.en: Beatriz lives in São Paulo and went to Salvador for the first time, because a childhood friend was getting married.
Her friend, Aline, had sent the address of her grandmother's house, where everyone was going to meet before the party.
The house was in an old neighborhood, near the center of the city.
Beatriz took a taxi at the hotel, but the driver dropped her off at the bottom of a huge steep street.

sentences.en: "Cars can't get through there, miss. Just go up and turn left," he said.
She climbed the street with her suitcase, with a very strong sun on her head.
At the top, however, there were three streets and two alleys, and none of them had a sign.
She tried to use the map on her phone, but there was no internet there.
Beatriz started to get worried, because the party would start at five and it was already four fifteen.
So she went into a small pharmacy on the corner and asked for help.
The owner of the pharmacy, a very friendly man, didn't know the name of the street.
"Here we don't really use street names," he explained, laughing.
"What's the landmark?" he asked.
Beatriz remembered that Aline had mentioned a blue church and a bakery famous for its cheese bread.
"Ah, Dona Lúcia's house!" said the man.
He closed the pharmacy for five minutes and went with her all the way there.
They crossed a square, passed in front of the blue church and went into a narrow alley.
At the end of the alley, there was a yellow house full of flowers and happy people.
Aline was very moved and said "thank you very much" to the man from the pharmacy.
Beatriz got to the party on time, although her face was red from the heat.
Since then, when someone asks for an address, she always asks first what the landmark is.

sentences.en: Rodrigo and his boyfriend, Diego, live in Porto Alegre and decided to spend a weekend on the coast.
They rented a house on a remote beach, about a hundred and fifty kilometers from the city.
They left on Saturday very early to avoid the traffic on the highway.
Diego was driving, and Rodrigo was in charge of the map and the music.
After the toll booth, however, they found the road closed because of a flood.
A police officer explained that the river had risen during the night and no one could cross the bridge.
He pointed to a yellow sign with the word "detour," toward the countryside.
The new route was longer and went through many small towns.
For an hour, they followed the signs with no problem.

Since they were already late anyway, the two decided to see the place.
The waterfall was beautiful, with clean water and almost no one around.
They swam, had a snack and only got to the beach at the end of the afternoon.
Now, whenever they disagree over a map, Diego says: "Sometimes the wrong way is the best."

sentences.en: Camila had finished university in December and was looking for her first job as an engineer.
For two months, she sent her résumé to more than thirty companies.
Almost no one answered, and she started to lose hope.
One day, however, she received an email from a solar energy company in Curitiba.
They wanted to do an interview with her on Friday, at nine in the morning.
Camila was happy, but also very nervous.
The day before, she read everything about the company and rehearsed her answers with her mother.
On Friday, although she was afraid of the traffic, she left home very early.
However, the bus broke down in the middle of the avenue.

tokens.en: to go down, to get off

sentences.en: The passengers had to get off and wait for another bus.
Camila looked at her watch: it was eight forty.
She called the company and explained the problem to the secretary.
The secretary said it wasn't a problem and that the boss could wait half an hour.

tokens.en: to get, to take, to catch

sentences.en: Even so, Camila decided to take a taxi so as not to arrive very late.
She arrived at ten past nine, tired and with a red face.
The boss, a friendly man named Ricardo, asked her to sit down and have a coffee.
He asked about the internship she had done and about her university projects.
Camila answered calmly, despite the morning's stress.
At the end, Ricardo said that he liked people who solve problems on their own.
"You didn't give up when the bus broke down; that's what we need," he explained.
Two weeks later, Camila signed the contract.
Today she works in the projects department and always leaves home an hour early.

sentences.en: At university, Professor Eduardo asked the class to do a team project on recycling.
The deadline was short: each team would have only three weeks to hand in the research and give a talk to the class.
Diego, Letícia, Bruno and Aline formed a team, although they didn't know each other well.
At the first meeting, they divided up the tasks and made a schedule in a spreadsheet.
Letícia was in charge of the data, Diego the writing and Aline the charts.
Bruno, who worked at night in a restaurant, said he would give the talk.
During the first week, everything went well.
In the second week, however, Bruno stopped answering the team's messages.
Diego got annoyed and wanted to tell the professor everything.
"Maybe he's having some problem," said Aline.
"Before complaining, we should talk to him."
So Letícia called Bruno many times, and he finally answered.
He explained that his father had gotten sick and that he was working overtime to pay the hospital.
He was embarrassed and didn't know how to tell his classmates.
The team decided to help: each one would speak a little in the talk.
Bruno, on the other hand, would do the charts on his phone, during lunch at the restaurant.
On the day of the talk, the four spoke confidently and answered all the questions.
The professor really liked the work and gave the team a grade of nine.
After class, they went to a restaurant near the university for dinner.
Bruno said his father was already better and said "thank you very much" to his classmates.
Since then, the four always study at Aline's house before exams.

questions.q: Sobre o que era o trabalho?
questions.qEn: What was the project about?

questions.q: Por que Bruno parou de responder?
questions.qEn: Why did Bruno stop answering?

questions.q: Que nota a equipe recebeu?
questions.qEn: What grade did the team get?

sentences.en: In Marcos's neighborhood, on the outskirts of Salvador, there was an old square next to the school.
In the past, the children played there and the elderly chatted under the trees.
In recent years, however, the square became dirty and forgotten.
The benches were broken, the lights were out and there was trash everywhere.
At night, nobody wanted to go through there, because of the lack of safety.
Marcos, a teacher at the school, got tired of complaining only to the neighbors.
He decided to call the residents to a meeting at the neighborhood church.
At the first meeting, only twelve people came, and many had no hope.
"City hall never listens to us. It's not worth it," said Seu Antônio.
Marcos, however, insisted and gave two ideas.
First, they would write an email to the mayor, with the signatures of all the residents.
Second, they would clean the square themselves, all together, on the weekend.
In two weeks, they got more than a thousand signatures.
On Saturday, more than a hundred people arrived with paint, plants and a great desire to work.
The young people painted the benches, the children planted flowers and the older ones helped sweep.
A TV journalist heard about the story and did a report.
The news aired on the evening news, and lots of people shared the report on social media.
Two days later, the mayor called Marcos and scheduled a visit to the neighborhood.
He said he would fix the lights and put more security in the square.
Many residents doubted it, because the mayor had already said the same thing before.
This time, however, the new lights arrived within a month.
Today, the square is full of children in the afternoon, and the elderly have gone back to chatting under the trees.
Seu Antônio admitted he was wrong and now is the first to arrive at the meetings.

questions.qEn: Where was the square?

sentences.en: There was one week left until the mayoral election in Manaus.
Gabriel was eighteen years old and was going to vote for the first time.
He wanted to choose well, so he read the news every day.
One night, his grandmother, Dona Lúcia, showed him a message on her phone, very upset.
"Look at this! This candidate is going to end pensions for the elderly!"
The message had a photo of the candidate and lots of words in big letters.
His grandmother had already shared the message with all her friends from church.
Gabriel found the news strange. There was no date, no newspaper name, no author.
"Before believing it, it's better that we check," he said.
He looked for the information online, in three well-known newspapers.
None of them said anything about it.
Then he found a group of journalists who investigate news from the internet.
There was the same message, with these words in red: "This is not true."
The journalists explained that the photo was old and that the candidate had never said that.
Dona Lúcia was embarrassed. "I believed it because it seemed true."
Gabriel explained that a lot of news like that is created to make people scared and angry.
"When we get angry, we share without thinking," he said.
His grandmother decided to do something. She sent a new message to her friends.
In the message, she explained the mistake and asked everyone to check news before sharing.
Some friends thanked her, but others got irritated and didn't believe her.
On election Sunday, Gabriel and his grandmother went to vote together.
Gabriel didn't tell who he was going to vote for, and neither did his grandmother.
But, on the way out, she said that, for the first time, she had chosen with information and not with fear.

questions.qEn: How old was Gabriel?

questions.q: O que a mensagem dizia sobre o candidato?
questions.qEn: What did the message say about the candidate?

sentences.en: At the office, everyone knew that Marcos was never on time.
He always arrived ten or fifteen minutes late and had a different excuse for each day.
One Friday, the boss, Patrícia, scheduled a very important meeting with a client from Lisbon.
The meeting would be on Monday, at eight in the morning sharp.
"I hope you arrive on time this time," she said, annoyed.
On Sunday night, Marcos set the alarm on his phone to ring at six and went to bed early.
In the early hours, however, a strong storm hit, with lots of lightning and thunder.
The power went out in the whole neighborhood, and the phone, which wasn't charged, died.
When Marcos opened his eyes, the sun was already high.
He looked at the kitchen clock and saw that it was seven forty.
He took a quick shower, put on the first clothes he found and ran out without having breakfast.
He arrived at the office at eight twenty, tired and hot.
To his surprise, the meeting room was empty.
The secretary explained that the client's flight had been delayed and that the meeting had been postponed to Tuesday.
Patrícia had sent a message on Sunday night, but his phone had no power.
Marcos was relieved, but also a little embarrassed.
On Tuesday, he arrived at the office at seven thirty, half an hour early.
When Patrícia came in and saw him there, she was so surprised she almost dropped her coffee.
The meeting was a success, and the client signed a two-year contract with the company.
Since then, Marcos has used his grandfather's old watch, which doesn't depend on power or the internet.
He still arrives late from time to time, but rarely more than five minutes.

questions.qEn: What time was the meeting?

questions.q: Por que Marcos não acordou na hora?
questions.qEn: Why didn't Marcos wake up on time?

questions.qEn: Why was the meeting postponed?

sentences.en: Fernanda and Eduardo have been married for ten years, but until last year they had never traveled to Europe.
At the start of the year, they decided that, in the long run, that would be the most important trip of the decade.
During the first half of the year, they saved a bit of their salary every month.
In February, they bought the tickets to Lisbon for the first two weeks of July.
Fernanda made an itinerary with museums, beaches and typical restaurants.
In April, however, Eduardo's boss gave some bad news.
The company had received a huge project, which had to be delivered by the end of the third quarter.
Because of that, no one on the team could take vacation in July.
Eduardo came home sad and told his wife everything.
Fernanda was frustrated, since she had waited for that trip for months.
"What if we postponed the trip to September?" asked Eduardo.
She thought that changing the tickets would be very expensive.
The next day, the two of them opened the airline's app and asked for information.
To their surprise, the fee was small: only three hundred reais per person.
Besides that, in September the hotels would be cheaper and the beaches would be less crowded.
The weather would also be good, neither too hot nor too cold.
So they changed the date and rented a small apartment near the river.
Eduardo worked a lot during the winter, including on some weekends.
The project was delivered two days before the deadline.
In September, at last, the two of them boarded for Lisbon.
On the first night, they had dinner at a typical restaurant, with wine and roast fish.
Fernanda said that she was happy to have waited.

sentences.en: Mariana wanted to throw a surprise party for her father's sixtieth birthday, in Curitiba.
She had chosen her grandmother's garden, which is full of flowers and trees.
For two weeks, she got everything ready very carefully.
She bought yellow and red tablecloths for the tables and lots of purple and white flowers.
Everyone knows that the weather in Curitiba changes very fast.
On the eve of the party, Mariana watched the weather forecast on TV.
The news announced drizzle in the morning and a strong storm in the afternoon, with lightning and thunder.
Her brother, Lucas, called, worried.
"Maybe it's better to have the party inside the house."
Mariana didn't agree, because the living room was small and dark.
"The forecast isn't always right. I hope the sky is blue tomorrow."
On Saturday, the day dawned cloudy and gray, but it wasn't raining.
The guests arrived at noon, and her father was very moved by the surprise.
Everyone ate, talked and danced in the colorful garden.
At three o'clock, however, the sky suddenly turned dark and it started to get very windy.
Soon after came the rain, with hail and lightning.
Everyone ran to the living room, carrying plates, glasses and chairs.
The yellow tablecloths got soaked, and the cake almost fell off the table.
Mariana was frustrated, but her father started to laugh.
"This is the most fun party of my life!"
In the small room, people got closer and sang with her father.
An hour later, the storm passed, and the sun came out between the clouds.
The sky turned blue again, and the leaves on the trees were green and wet.

Mariana realized that the rain had made the party even more joyful.

sentences.en: Seu Antônio has been painting houses in Paraty for more than thirty years.
He knows the town's climate well: hot, humid and with lots of rain in the summer.
One day, a couple from São Paulo bought an old house near the sea.
The wife, Beatriz, asked Seu Antônio to paint the house.
"I want everything dark gray, with black windows. It's very modern."
Seu Antônio went quiet and looked at the sky.
"Are you sure? The sun here is very strong. A dark house is going to get very hot."
He also explained that, with the humidity, the dark paint would fade in a short time.
Beatriz got irritated. She thought he knew nothing about modern houses.
"I'm paying, and I choose the color," she said.
Seu Antônio said nothing more and started the job.
That summer, however, a very strong heat wave came.
For three weeks, the temperature went over 38 degrees.
Inside the gray house, the air was stuffy, and nobody could sleep.
The couple ran the cold air all day, and the electricity bill came very high.
Then came the rainy season, and the gray paint soon became faded and ugly.
At the end of the year, Beatriz called Seu Antônio, a little embarrassed.
"You were right. What do you think we should do?"
He said that a soft white would make the house less hot.
"And to have a bold color, we can paint the door turquoise."
Beatriz really liked his opinion.
In March, the job was finished: the house was white, with a turquoise door and blue windows.

sentences.en: Now people stop in the street to take photos of the house.
And Seu Antônio always says: in Paraty, it's the sun that chooses the color.

sentences.en: Mariana had been a teacher at a public school on the outskirts of Salvador for ten years.
Every year she noticed the same problem: the students wanted to read, but had no books at home.
The school library was basic and had few books, almost all of them old and out of date.

sentences.en: One day she decided to undertake a bold project: to create a library for the whole community, in an empty house in the neighborhood.
The owner, a retired gentleman, agreed to lend the property for five years, provided that the renovation was done by the residents.
To make the project possible, Mariana needed to raise at least forty thousand reais.
She called parents, students and neighbors to a meeting in the square.
“If we wait for the government, our children will grow up without books,” she stressed.
Each person took on a role: Rafael, who studied at the university, was in charge of social media.
Dona Lúcia, retired, started making cakes and cheese bread for the Sunday market, and all the profit went to the project.
A group of parents offered to fix the doors and windows and paint the house.
Mariana, meanwhile, wrote to publishers and companies asking for books and money.
Many didn't reply, and some sent curt answers.

sentences.en: A big publisher, however, agreed to send two thousand books, as long as the library opened before December.
The deadline was tight, and the renovation was behind schedule.

sentences.en: In October, they still hadn't raised even half the money, and some people gave up.
Mariana got discouraged and even considered postponing everything until the following year.
It was Rafael who convinced her not to give up.
He recorded a short film of the students reading the school's few books and talking about what they wanted to be when they grew up.
The film was shared thousands of times and even reached the press.
In ten days, the group received more money than in four months.
With the money, they managed to speed up the renovation and finish everything three days before the deadline.
On the day the library opened, the street was full of children, parents and grandparents.
The two thousand books arrived by truck, and the students helped put each one in the right place.
A journalist asked Mariana what she had learned from all of that.
“That nobody does anything alone,” she answered. “I just asked for help; it was the community that made the library.”
Today the library opens Monday to Saturday and offers writing and Portuguese classes for adults.
Now Mariana aspires to open another one in a nearby neighborhood.
She knows it will be hard, but she learned that when the community wants it, what seemed unfeasible can become real.

sentences.en: Juliana had just been hired as a manager at a delivery company in Curitiba.
In her first week, the company's president, Eduardo, called Juliana into his office.
“Our customers have been complaining about delays for months, and nobody can explain why,” he said.
“I want you to look into what is happening and bring me a report by the end of the month.”
Juliana started by talking to the drivers, who complained about the traffic and the wrong addresses.
Then she spent days studying the delivery spreadsheets for the last six months.
The data was confusing and inconsistent: some orders had two delivery dates, and others had none.
Little by little, she realized that the problem wasn't in the streets, but inside the office.
The app the company used to choose routes was obsolete and didn't take rush hour into account.
As a result, drivers were sent onto jammed avenues at the hours of heaviest traffic.
Besides, she uncovered something nobody expected.
A fuel supplier was charging exorbitant prices, and the contracts had been signed without any tender.
The contracts were linked to a long-standing partner in the company, Marcos, who was very close to Eduardo.
When Juliana showed the report to Eduardo, he was uncomfortable.

sentences.en: “Maybe it's better not to mention the supplier for now,” he said. “Let's talk only about the app.”
Juliana weighed it up for a few seconds.

sentences.en: She knew she was risking her job, but she also knew that a report without that information wouldn't be honest.

sentences.en: “I understand your concern,” she replied, “but you asked me to shed light on the delays, and the price of fuel is tied to the same problem.”

sentences.en: She stressed that she didn't want to condemn anyone, only to show the numbers.
Eduardo was silent for a long minute.
Then he asked her to extend the report's deadline by a week, so that he could talk to Marcos.
Juliana used the week to think about what to do next.
She decided that the obsolete app would be replaced and that the drivers would help choose the routes.
She also delegated to two interns the task of correcting the wrong addresses in the database.
The following week, Eduardo announced to the team that the contract with the supplier would be canceled and that the company would hold a new tender.
Marcos left the company shortly afterwards, without making a scene.
Three months later, the delays had fallen by almost half, and customers complained much less.
Eduardo called Juliana into his office again, this time to offer her a raise.
“You could have done what I asked and kept quiet,” he said. “Thank goodness you didn't.”

sentences.en: Carla was forty-two and a renowned lawyer in São Paulo.
She had been sleeping badly for months, but she thought the insomnia was just tiredness.
She left the office after midnight and woke up at five to answer emails.
Lately, besides the insomnia, she had migraines almost every day and sometimes a strange nausea.
One Monday, during an important meeting, Carla felt very dizzy and almost fainted.
A colleague called an ambulance, and she was taken to the emergency room.
The doctor on duty, a calm and polite woman, asked many questions about her daily life.
“You have hypertension, and your blood pressure is very high for your age,” said the doctor.
“Besides, the symptoms you feel are typical of burnout.”
Carla felt embarrassed, as if she had been caught doing something wrong.
“I can't stop now,” she argued. “In two months I'm going to become a partner at the firm.”
The doctor explained that chronic hypertension, if it didn't receive treatment, could worsen other problems, including in the heart and the brain.
She prescribed a medicine for the blood pressure and said that Carla needed at least a month off.
“The medicine's side effect is mild, but no pill will cure the exhaustion of someone who never rests.”
That night, at home, Carla stayed awake until late, thinking about what the doctor had said.
She remembered that her father had died early, of a heart problem, and that the doctor had asked whether the disease was hereditary in the family.
She called her sister, Patrícia, and opened up for the first time in years.
“I always thought my body would never get sick,” said Carla.
Patrícia, who was a nurse, wasn't surprised.
“You're sedentary, you eat badly and you sleep four hours a night. Your body is warning you.”
The next day, Carla asked for a meeting with the head of the firm.
She was afraid that the time off would mean the end of her career.
The boss listened to everything without saying a word and then told her he had been hospitalized because of his heart at fifty.
“The partner position can wait a month. Your health can't,” he said.
Carla spent that month away from the office.
She started walking every morning, learned to cook healthy meals and went back to reading novels.
Her blood pressure improved little by little, and the headaches became rarer and rarer.
When she went back to work, she delegated more tasks to the interns and started leaving the office before seven.
Some colleagues thought she was less ambitious.
Carla, however, had never felt so good.
“If I hadn't fainted in that meeting, maybe I'd be in the hospital now,” she thought.

sentences.en: For a year Thiago had been running every morning, thinking about the big street race in Porto Alegre.
He was thirty-five, an engineer, and until two years earlier he had been a sedentary man with obesity.
Running had changed his life: he had lost twenty kilos and now had much more stamina.
With three weeks to go before the race, however, he fell on a wet sidewalk and hurt his ankle.
At first he thought it was just a bruise, because he could still walk.
At night, however, the ankle was swollen and purple, and Thiago could barely stand.
His girlfriend, Aline, insisted that he go to the emergency room.
After three hours of waiting, a young doctor looked at his foot and ordered a scan.
The scan showed a small fracture and inflammation in the joint.
“No running for at least two months,” said the doctor, as he wrote a prescription for a painkiller.
Thiago was crushed. “But the race is in three weeks! I can't give up now.”
The doctor explained that if he ran with his ankle like that, he could be left with lasting damage forever.
“An untreated injury today can turn into chronic pain ten years from now.”
In the first weeks, Thiago stayed home, irritated and bored.
He watched races on TV and felt envy and frustration at the same time.
Aline tried to help, but his replies were more and more curt.
One night she got angry: “You talk as if running were more important than your health and than the people who love you.”
Thiago didn't answer, but he knew she was right.
The following week, he started physiotherapy three times a week.
The treatment was slow and sometimes it hurt, but Thiago liked feeling that he was getting better.
He learned exercises for his hips and legs which, according to the team, could prevent new injuries.
On the day of the race, Thiago went to the avenue, but not to run.
Together with Aline, he stood at the edge of the route, handing out water to the people running past.
He saw friends arrive tired and elated and, to his surprise, he didn't feel envy.
Two months later, the ankle had healed, and he gradually went back to running.
The next race would be in October, and this time he was going to listen to his body before listening to the clock.
Aline joked: “If you fall again, I'll personally forbid you to leave the house.”
Thiago laughed and said that this time he would be more sensible.

sentences.en: Luíza was twenty-nine and worked as a soap opera scriptwriter, but what she really wanted was to make her own films.
For two years, on her days off and at weekends, she wrote and shot a twenty-minute short film.
The plot came from the stories her grandmother used to tell about the folklore of the Amazon.
In the film, a girl from Manaus gets lost in the forest and is helped by characters from folklore.
Everything was made on a tiny budget: the costumes were made by Luíza's aunt, and the soundtrack was recorded by her cousin on a guitar.
The lead was a girl from the neighborhood who had never done theater or film.
In May, to everyone's surprise, the short was chosen for the Brasília film festival.
Luíza was elated, but also apprehensive.
It would be the first time the film would be seen by strangers and by critics.
On opening night, the theater was full.
During the twenty minutes of film, Luíza couldn't watch the film; she watched people's faces.
Some laughed at the funny scenes; others seemed bored.
At the ending, when the girl returns to her grandmother's house, a lady near the stage cried.
The audience applauded for almost a minute.
The next day, however, a well-known critic published a harsh review.
He wrote that the plot was banal, that the characters were crude, and that the film looked like a school project.
Luíza read the review three times and spent the day in her hotel room, disappointed.
She called her grandmother in Manaus and poured her heart out.
“That man knows a lot about cinema, but he doesn't know the forest,” said her grandmother. “Don't let a critic decide whether your story is good.”
On the last day of the festival, there was a twist.
Luíza's short was chosen by the audience as the best film of the festival.
When she went up on stage, Luíza could barely speak.
She said the film belonged to her grandmother, her aunt, her cousin and the girl who played the lead.
Afterwards, many people asked the girl for autographs, and she was embarrassed and happy.
A film businessman approached Luíza and asked if she had a script for a feature film.
She didn't, but she said yes.
That night, at the hotel, she began to write.
Months later, the same critic wrote a column about the festival and admitted that Luíza's short had been the surprise of the year.
Luíza kept both reviews.
“One reminds me that I still have a lot to learn; the other, that it's worth carrying on.”

In the 1960s, she had been acclaimed all over Brazil, but during the dictatorship her songs were banned by the censors.
She never recorded again, and the neighborhood almost forgot her name.
It was her granddaughter, Camila, who brought her grandmother's collection to the school: photos, stage clothes and old recordings.
Diego spent nights listening to those recordings, and every song moved him more.
The samba he wrote spoke of freedom, of longing and of the hillside community where she had been born.
Rehearsals began in September, in the school's street, with hundreds of residents.
The women of the community spent months making the costumes by hand, in shades of blue and silver, the singer's favorite colors.
Unlike the big schools, theirs had a tiny budget and relied on volunteer work.
On the night of the parade, the avenue was packed, and Diego's school was the first to go in.
Everything was going well until, a few meters from the start of the avenue, the main float, with Dona Lúcia's face painted in gold, broke down.
Diego felt his heart stop.
Without the float, the school would get a low score.
For a few minutes, nobody knew what to do.
It was then that Camila started singing the samba alone, in the middle of the avenue.
The school's band followed her, then the whole school, then the audience.
Thirty thousand people were singing the name of a woman the country had forgotten.
The float was pushed by dozens of men, and the parade went on.
When the scores were announced, days later, the school came fifth, far from first.
Even so, the parade was the most talked-about of Carnival.
A critic wrote in a column that it had been the most moving moment he had seen on the avenue in twenty years.
Within a few weeks, Dona Lúcia's songs were being played again at parties, in bars and on music apps.
A publisher decided to publish a book about her life.
And the city hall announced the heritage listing of the house where she had been born, which became a small museum.
Diego still gets emotional when he remembers that night.

So she called her father, in Florianópolis, who agreed to help without thinking twice.

sentences.en: Sofia had a small but well-known restaurant in the historic center of Recife.
After fifteen years, the head cook had retired, and she needed to hire another before Carnival.
She received dozens of résumés, but only two candidates made it to the last stage.

His résumé was wide-ranging and full of famous names.
In the cooking test, he made a fish with orange and pepper sauce, on a matte black plate.
The dish was sophisticated, beautiful and, without a doubt, tasty.

With the other kitchen staff, Bruno was curt and overbearing.
When a young waiter dropped a spoon, Bruno called him useless in front of everyone.
Later, when Sofia asked about the restaurant's menu, his answers were vague and ambiguous.
“I would do everything from scratch,” he said. “This menu is old-fashioned and a bit banal.”

She was only twenty-six and had worked only in a neighborhood bar and in her grandmother's kitchen.
In the test, she was hesitant at first and asked if she could taste the house seasonings.
Then she made a simple fish broth, but with a deep and subtle flavor.
She was meticulous: she cleaned the counter at every step and explained every choice.
With the staff, she was friendly and patient, and even helped the waiter wash the dishes.
When Sofia asked what she would change on the menu, the answer was brief and to the point.
“I would change almost nothing. Customers come back here because they feel at home.”
“Maybe I'd just add more vegetables from the market and drop the dessert that nobody orders.”
That night, Sofia talked with her husband, Paulo, who was a food critic.
“Bruno knows a lot; his dish was the best I've eaten this year,” Paulo admitted.

The second, in Ipanema, was modern and sophisticated, with a huge window facing the sea.
But the building fee alone cost almost as much as the rent of the first one.
The third was the most peculiar.
It was an apartment in an old, heritage-listed building, in a neighborhood far from the center, with tall windows and stone stairs.
The owner, an eighty-year-old man who had been an artist, lived on the ground floor.
He welcomed the couple with coffee and cake and told, with nostalgia, the story of the building.
The apartment was pretty but in poor condition: the shower didn't heat up, and the paint was faded.
“I charge a low rent, as long as you take good care of the place,” said the man.
Felipe got excited, but Camila was more sensible.
“A renovation is going to be expensive, and we're the ones who pay.”
The other three properties were easy to dismiss: one was in a dark alley, another was next to a noisy overpass, and the last cost more than the two of them earned per month.
At the end of the week, they still hadn't chosen anything.
That was when something unexpected happened.
The old man called Felipe: “My grandson is a plumber. If you want, he'll do the repairs on the shower and the kitchen, and I'll pay half.”

sentences.en: Eduardo inherited an old neighborhood bar on a corner in Belo Horizonte from his uncle.
For forty years, the place was famous for its bar snacks and its always ice-cold beer.
But when Eduardo started running the place, he noticed that almost everything in the kitchen was industrially made.
The ham came in plastic packaging, the sauce came ready-made, and the French fries arrived frozen.
He read the packaging and was alarmed by the amount of preservatives.
Eduardo had studied gastronomy and dreamed of a real kitchen.
So he decided to replace the ultra-processed foods with food made right there.
He went looking for suppliers in the countryside, two hours from the city.
There he met Mrs. Lúcia, who grows organic vegetables without any pesticide.
She grew everything by hand, as her mother and grandmother had done.
"My harvest depends on the rain, my son," she warned. "Some months there's a lot, some months there's nothing."
Eduardo thought he could handle that.
The first months were a success.
The dishes were simple, but they tasted like home cooking.
The customers loved the grilled chicken, the crispy potatoes and the bean broth seasoned on the spot.
In August, however, the drought came.
The lack of rain wiped out half the harvest, and the supply became a problem.
Some weeks, there were no tomatoes; in others, there were no onions.
Besides, organic vegetables are perishable and don't last many days in the fridge.
The cook, Mr. Antônio, who had worked there for twenty years, got irritated.
"With your uncle, we never ran out of anything!" he complained.
Eduardo thought about backing down, but had another idea.
Instead of a menu that never changes, the bar would start having a board with the dishes of the day.
If there were carrots, there would be carrot soup; if there were tomatoes, there would be chicken in tomato sauce.
Mr. Antônio was skeptical, but little by little he started to enjoy creating new dishes.
The customers changed too and started asking, right at the door: "What's on today?"
Today, Eduardo's bar is always packed on weekends.
And the beer, of course, is still as cold as in his uncle's time.

sentences.en: Maria had been a public school teacher for thirty-two years and had been retired since 2015.
Her grandson, Pedro, was twenty-four and worked freelance, with no formal employment contract and no paid holidays.
The two lived in the same apartment in São Paulo and talked about everything, including politics.
That year, the government announced a pension reform.
According to the government, the minimum retirement age would go up, and the pensions of those already receiving them would rise less than inflation.
The teachers' union called a strike and a big demonstration on Paulista Avenue.
Maria, at seventy, decided to go.
“I worked my whole life. I'm not going to stay home while they mess with my pension,” she said.
Pedro was worried about his grandmother's health, but he also had a different opinion.
“Grandma, I understand your outrage, but the numbers don't add up.”
“The population is getting older, and fewer and fewer young people pay into the pension system.”
“If nothing changes, when I'm your age, maybe there won't be any pension at all for me.”
Maria listened to her grandson without interrupting.
Then she admitted that the pension system needed to change, but questioned who was going to foot the bill.

tokens.en: to charge; to demand, pressure (for results)

sentences.en: “Why is it always the poor and the teachers? Why not charge more taxes to the richest?”
Pedro didn't know how to answer.
On the day of the protest, he ended up going with her, so that she wouldn't go alone.
The avenue was packed with teachers, nurses, students and retirees.
Pedro, who had gone only to look after his grandmother, was surprised by what he saw.
A nurse said she worked at two hospitals to pay the rent; a bus driver said that with the new law, he would work until seventy.
For the first time, Pedro realized that the reform wasn't just numbers in a spreadsheet, but the lives of millions of people.
In the months that followed, the reform was in every headline.
After a lot of pressure, the deputies passed the reform with important changes.
The minimum age went up, but less than the government wanted, and those who were already retired lost nothing.
The president signed the law in December.
Maria wasn't satisfied, but she wasn't discouraged either.
“It wasn't everything we wanted, but if nobody had taken to the streets, it would have been much harder.”
Pedro, for his part, started paying into the pension system as a freelancer and reading more about politics.
Today, he and his grandmother still disagree now and then.
But he learned from her that citizenship doesn't end at the ballot box: it continues in the street, in the press and in kitchen conversations.

sentences.en: At the top of the main church in a small town in Minas Gerais, there is a clock almost a hundred years old.
In the old days, it was what told everyone the time for church, the market, school and lunch.
But, in the early hours of a winter morning, the clock stopped at a quarter past three and didn't move again.
At the time, almost nobody noticed.
The older people complained for a week and then forgot.
After all, everyone has the right time on their phone.
It was Sofia, a ten-year-old girl, who asked the question no one had asked.
"Why is the church clock always at the same time?" she asked her grandfather, Mr. Antônio.
Her grandfather laughed, but the question stayed with him for days.
In his youth, he had helped the old caretaker look after the clock.
He still remembered every part up there at the top of the church.
He went to the city hall and asked if he could try to fix the clock.
The secretary in charge said that, previously, an engineer from Belo Horizonte had already made an estimate.
The price was too high for the town, and the project had been postponed indefinitely.
Mr. Antônio offered his own time, without charging anything, as long as the city hall paid for the parts.
The permit was granted on a provisional basis, valid for six months.
Every Saturday, he climbed the church's narrow staircase, and Sofia went along.
At the same time, he cleaned the parts and explained to his granddaughter what each one did.
The work went on slowly, in stages, and every now and then it seemed endless.
In April, only one part was missing, which had to be made by an old man from the countryside.
Finally, on a Sunday morning, the clock started running again.
When the clock struck noon, people came out of their houses and looked up, surprised.
Some cried, because they hadn't heard that clock for more than eight years.
Later, the city hall named the square after Mr. Antônio.
Today, Sofia is twenty and she is the one who climbs the stairs every Saturday.
Time passes anyway, but there are those who make sure it is heard.

sentences.en: In the morning weather forecast, the weather service had announced a mild day, with sun between the clouds.
Larissa, who worked as a journalist at a São Paulo newspaper, left home in a light shirt, without thinking about rain.
At three in the afternoon, however, the sky began to turn greyish, and the humidity made the air muggy.
From the office window, on the tenth floor, she saw dark, almost purple clouds coming from the south.
At four, it began to thunder, and a gust of wind carried chairs and signs along the avenue.
Soon after came a downpour so heavy that you couldn't see the other side of the street.
The city hall asked people on social media not to leave the buildings.
Larissa's boss, Gustavo, looked at her and said: “You live near the river, don't you? How about doing the report on the flooding?”
She hesitated for a moment, because the rain still hadn't stopped.
But it was her job, and she knew people needed reliable information.
By subway and then on foot, she reached her neighborhood almost an hour later, completely soaked.
The scene was sad: the brown water had risen more than a meter and gotten into the houses and shops.
Cars were stuck in the middle of the water, and an empty bus was stopped at the intersection.
Dona Lúcia, a seventy-year-old neighbor, was at the window on the second floor, distressed.
“My fridge, my sofa, everything ended up under water,” she said, crying.
“Every year the same thing happens, and the city hall talks about works that never get off the ground.”
Larissa recorded interviews with residents and wrote everything down on her phone, with ice-cold hands.
The "feels like" temperature had dropped almost ten degrees in two hours.
At night, when the cold front passed, the sky cleared, with a strange, almost pretty bluish tone.
Larissa's report was published the next day and shared thousands of times.
She didn't write only about the rain, but also about the garbage in the streets and the lack of maintenance of the city's rivers.
A city councillor responded by saying that the problem was the rain, not the city.
Larissa found the answer inconsistent: “If it rains like this every March, it's not a surprise; it's a lack of care.”
A week later, Dona Lúcia called Larissa.
“After your report, they sent a team to clean the river. It's not much, but it's something.”
Larissa was happy, but she knew the next storm would arrive before the works.
Since that day, she has never again left home without looking at the sky twice.

sentences.en: Beatriz lived in a small town in Minas Gerais and dyed clothes with dyes made from plants, flowers and earth.
Her shirts had soft, simple colors: a yellowish tone from flowers, a reddish brown from earth, a blue that was almost grey from leaves.
She hated the garish colors of the mall stores and said that every shade had a story.
Customers from São Paulo and Rio bought her clothes online and paid well.
That year, however, the dry spell lasted much longer than in other years.
From May to October it didn't rain a single day, and the river that ran behind her house almost dried up.
The plants she used for dyeing turned dry and pale before flowering.
Besides, the little water in the river was dirty, and the dyes came out dull, lifeless.
Beatriz tried other recipes, but the colors stayed sad and greyish.
An old customer sent a message: “The last shirts faded after two times in the washing machine.”
Beatriz was embarrassed and gave the money back.
For the first time, she thought about giving up and buying industrial dyes.
“It would be easier and cheaper,” she told her brother, Diego, who had a farm nearby.
Diego, however, had a different opinion.
“The drought is changing the landscape; maybe your colors need to change too.”
He took his sister for a walk through the savanna around the farm.
Even at the end of the dry spell, she saw hues she had never noticed.
The earth was a strong red, the trees had silvery leaves and the sky, at dusk, turned golden and lilac.
Beatriz went home with her backpack full of leaves, stones and earth in ten different shades.
For weeks she mixed, boiled and dyed, and wrote each recipe in a notebook.
With the little water she had, she learned not to waste even a glass.
The new shirts weren't soft like the old ones: they were strong, warm and vibrant, with nuances of red and orange.
She named the collection Drought.
At first she was afraid the customers wouldn't like the change.

sentences.en: But the collection sold out in two weeks.

Beatriz was relieved, but she didn't go back to the old colors.
“The drought taught me to see what I didn't see,” she wrote in the notebook.
“Now I dye with what the earth gives me, not with what I wanted it to give me.”
